pairs.rationale: Both openings name Paul, Silvanus and Timothy and address the Thessalonian Church in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The second letter says our Father; the first says the Father and includes grace and peace in that unit. The repeated sender and addressee formula does not merge the letters or their occasions.

Both greet the recipients with grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The same named greeting sources occur in letters to different receiving communities; the repeated formula is a verbal parallel rather than evidence of one delivery occasion.

The reported increase of love for one another corresponds to the earlier letter's petition that the Lord make such love increase and overflow. The thanksgiving also names growing faith; the petition extends love to all and uses a wish rather than a report. Those additional scope and grammatical differences remain distinct.

Both associate boasting, affliction and endurance or perseverance. Thessalonians boasts of the recipients among God's Churches for the faith and endurance with which they bear persecution; Romans says we boast in afflictions because they produce perseverance and proven character. The objects of boasting and the explanatory chain differ.

Both connect affliction or suffering with God's kingdom. Acts reports encouragement to continue in faith because entry into the kingdom involves many afflictions; Thessalonians describes suffering for that kingdom and being counted worthy in God's righteous judgment. The encouragement and judgment descriptions remain distinct.

God's just repayment of affliction to those afflicting the readers corresponds to Romans reserving vengeance and repayment to the Lord. Romans commands readers not to avenge themselves; Thessalonians describes God's repayment. The actors and statement-versus-command roles remain separate.

Both portray revelation or coming with angels. Thessalonians names the Lord Jesus revealed from heaven with the angels of His power and relief for afflicted people; Matthew names the Son of Man coming with all angels and sitting on His glorious throne. Neither passage's added location, relief or throne detail is inserted into the other.

The flame-of-fire and vengeance language has a specific counterpart in Isaiah's description of the Lord coming like fire. Isaiah also names chariots like a storm, wrath and rejection; Thessalonians specifies those not knowing God or obeying the Lord Jesus' gospel. This is a scriptural image comparison rather than an identical account of every agent and circumstance.

The Lord-and-glory-of-His-strength formula closely corresponds to Isaiah's judgment scene. Isaiah describes handmade things carried into caves, rock clefts and earth holes from the Lord's terror and the glory of His strength; Thessalonians names eternal destruction from the Lord's presence and the glory of His strength. The different objects and predicates, and the actual from wording, remain without deciding its spatial or causal interpretation.

Both associate being glorified with holy ones or saints. The Psalm says God is glorified in the council of holy ones; Thessalonians describes the Lord's future coming to be glorified in His saints and marveled at among believers. The council and the believing recipients are not simply identified as one group, and the Psalm does not reproduce the coming-day statement.

Both prayers combine worthy language, good works and divine power. Thessalonians asks God to count the recipients worthy of calling and fulfill good resolve and faith's work with power; Colossians asks knowledge of His will toward a worthy walk, fruitful good work and empowerment for endurance and patience with joy. The petitions and stated effects remain distinct.

Jesus' statement in John that He has been glorified in those given to Him is a specific counterpart to the prayer that His name may be glorified in the readers. Thessalonians also names the readers in Him and grace; John states His own glorification in them. The perfect statement and the prayer's purpose, name wording and reciprocal addition are preserved.
